subject: ophthalmology
title: Visual pathway lesions and visual fields

steps.tx: The visual pathway runs from the **retina** through the optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate body and optic radiations to the visual cortex. Where a lesion sits along this route determines the field defect and whether the pupillary light reflex is affected. Localising the lesion is the core skill tested in exams, so learn the sequence first.

steps.tx: A **bitemporal hemianopia** is the classic sign of a central chiasmal lesion. The most common cause is a **pituitary adenoma**, which compresses the chiasm from below and damages the nasal fibres. Craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma also produce this pattern. Pituitary tumours are the commonest cause overall, so always check fields in a patient with headache and a sellar mass.

right.title: Post-chiasmal lesion
points: No optic atrophy beyond geniculate body

steps.tx: Lesions of the **optic tract** cause an incongruous homonymous hemianopia and produce **Wernicke's hemianopic pupil**, where the light reflex is lost when light falls on the temporal retina of the affected side. Lesions beyond the lateral geniculate body, including the optic radiations and visual cortex, leave the pupillary reflex normal because the pupillary fibres have already left the tract.

vis.alt: Diagram showing the visual pathway. An optic tract lesion causes incongruous homonymous hemianopia and affects the pupillary reflex (Wernicke's pupil). Lesions after the lateral geniculate body spare the pupillary reflex.
vis.caption: Optic tract lesion: incongruous hemianopia, Wernicke's pupil. Post-LGN: normal pupils

steps.tx: Within the **optic radiations**, fibres are split by their course. Inferior fibres in the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) carry the upper visual field, so a temporal lesion gives a **superior quadrantanopia**. Superior fibres in the parietal lobe carry the lower field, giving an inferior quadrantanopia. Complete parieto-occipital damage gives a full homonymous hemianopia, often with **macular sparing** due to dual MCA and PCA supply.

Inferior fibres in the temporal lobe, known as Meyer's loop, carry the upper visual field, so a temporal lesion gives a superior quadrantanopia. Superior fibres in the parietal lobe carry the lower field, giving an inferior quadrantanopia. steps.tx: In **cortical blindness**, bilateral occipital infarction removes vision while pupillary light reflexes stay normal. Patients may deny blindness, which is **Anton syndrome**, and may perceive moving but not static targets, the **Riddoch phenomenon**. Visual evoked responses are extinguished, which separates cortical blindness from hysteria, where these responses are normal.
